Tympanosclerosis and atherosclerosis plaques:  a comparative analytical study on some new microbiological  and immunohistochemical aspects
Shadman Nemati1  · Alia Saberi1  · Ali Faghih Habibi1  · Hossein Hemmati2  · Reza Jafari‐Shakib3,4  ·  Mojtaba Hedayati Ch5  · Elahe Bozorgzadeh4,6
Received: 30 September 2020 / Accepted: 20 October 2020  © Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2020
Abstract Purpose The aim of this study was to compare chemical contents, expression of BMP-8a, and the presence of Mycoplasma  and ExoS-ExoU exotoxins producing Pseudomonas aeruginosa in tympanosclerosis (TS) and atherosclerosis (AS) plaques. Methods Thirty-six cases with TS and AS plaques (18 each) were selected and examined for chemical, immunohistochemi- cal, and microbial analysis. SPSS ver. 21 and t test analysis were used for comparing the findings, and the level of significance  was considered as p < 0.05. Results TS plaques showed lower carbon, higher calcium, and phosphorous contents compared to AS plaques (p value < 0.05).  Chlorine was detected in AS plaques (1.8 w%) which could probably be due to the presence of myeloperoxidase (MPO) in  atherosclerotic artery. Contrary to spherical shape of the surface of TS plaques, AS plaques were needle shaped. BMP-8a  expression in TS plaques (59.5%) was significantly higher (p value < 0.0001) than AS plaques (20%). Of the 18 TS specimens,  12, 14, and 3 were positive for ExoS, ExoU Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Mycoplasma genes, respectively, while of the 18  AS specimens, 2, 2, and 3 were positive for ExoS, ExoU Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Mycoplasma genes, respectively. Conclusion TS plaques are different from AS plaques in terms of elemental components, surface morphology, and BMP- 8a expression. Therefore, different calcification process and pathogenesis may be responsible for these two diseases. The  results of our study showed that both TS and AS plaques have genetic footprint of Mycoplasma, but the level of calcium  concentration-dependent exotoxins genes was found only in TS plaques.
Keywords Tympanosclerosis · Atherosclerosis · Scanning electron microscopy · Pseudomonas aeruginosa · BMP-8a
Introduction
Tympanosclerosis (TS) is a disorder of the middle-ear cav- ity where hyaline calcareous sediments are found on the  tympanic membrane, ossicular chain, and ligaments and  occasionally in the middle ear and mastoid surfaces [1].

TS plaques within the tympanic membrane often appear  as a semicircular crescent white plaque within the tym- panic membrane [2]. The prevalence of tympanosclerosis  in chronic otitis media (COM) has been reported from 9 to  38%. Relative to the quantity of calcification and its distur- bance of the ossicular chain movement, the patients experi- ence different degrees of conductive hearing loss. The etiol- ogy of TS has not been revealed completely [3]. However,  infection, physical trauma, myringotomy incisions, applica- tion of ventilation tube, chemical agents, metabolic changes,  genetic factors, and immunological reactions are considered  as responsible factors for this disease [4].
Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease  characterized by accumulation of lipids together with pen- etration of immunocytes, inflammatory cells, and calcium  deposits in the walls of medium and large-sized arteries,  wherein the arterial walls become thicker and lose their elas- ticity [5]. Endothelial cells, intimate smooth muscle cells,  and leukocytes have key roles in the progress of AS [6].  AS is a slow advancing and progressive disease, starting  from childhood. Various factors have been suggested as the  cause of this disease including hyperlipidemia, hypertension,  smoking, infection with bacteria and viruses, diabetes mel- litus, obesity, and genetic and habitual factors [7, 8].
Although TS and AS appears in two different organs,  they share similar histopathological and physiopathological  elements, and historically, many experts have known these  two processes as identical [9]. In both diseases, it is not  precisely recognized what starts the lesion principally [10].  Interestingly, some previous studies revealed relationship  between these diseases, and showed that AS patients had sta- tistically significant rate of TS in comparison to the normal  population. Pirodda et al. showed around 22.5% of hyper- cholesterolemia patients (4.9% in control subjects) and 36%  of patients underwent carotid endarterectomy (12% in con- trol group) had TS on otoscopy [10, 11]. In another study,  homocysteine, low-density lipoprotein, total cholesterol, and  triglyceride levels in 61 COM patients with TS plaques were  higher compared with those without TS plaques (p < 0.05)  and right and left internal carotid artery intima-media thick- ness was greater significantly (p = 0.001). In conclusion,  AS and TS were associated with identical risk factors [12].  These studies emphasized that there must be similar risk  factors triggering pathogenesis in both diseases [13].
TS is a progressive disorder, which appears to be the  main response of the tympanic membrane pars tensa to pro- longed sterile otitis media with effusion [14], and most of  the patients suffering from TS have earlier exposure to recur- rent serous otitis media (SOM), acute otitis media (AOM),  or chronic otitis media (COM) [15]. According to previous  studies, nitric oxide, free oxygen radicals, and catalase may  have a role in the development of TS in COM [16, 17]. Some  other studies revealed that the alteration in expressions of
transforming growth factor β1 (TGF-β1) and matrix metal- loproteinase-9 (MMP-9) involved in the formation of TS,  which may represent an important mechanism underlying  the pathogenesis of TS [18, 19]. Another study declared that  an association between C. pneumoniae or H. pylori infection  and the development of TS or other types of COM could not  be established [3]. Also, it has been generally believed that  bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Mycoplasma  pneumoniae involve in AOM and COM as well as in occur- rence of inflammatory process such as AS. Mycoplasma  pneumonia causes common respiratory tract infections, and  up to one-third of patients with Mycoplasma pneumonia  infection may have ear infection, although without positive  middle-ear fluid PCR [19]. This may partly be caused by dif- ficulties in culturing this fastidious organism. Nevertheless,  otitis media is often mentioned as a clinical condition asso- ciated with serologically verified M. pneumoniae infection.  Many studies in the past have shown the presence of Myco- plasma in cardiovascular diseases and middle-ear infections  in children and adults [20, 21].
The toxins such as ExoS and ExoU which are secreted  by type 3 secretion system (T3SS) of bacteria are the key  component responsible for TS, AOM, and COM [22, 23].
Due to development of calcification in both diseases,  evaluation of bone remodeling markers is a priority for  understanding the pathogenesis of these diseases. Different  factors influence differentiation and activation of osteoblasts,  and one of the most important ones is bone morphogenetic  proteins (BMPs). BMPs are the largest family of the TGF-β  superfamily and originally were recognized for their abil- ity in induction of bone formation, but it has known they  expressed in many tissues and have a role in a wide range  of processes including cellular proliferation and differen- tiation, adipogenesis, skeletal development, formation and  maintenance of vascular systems, and cancers [24]. A few  studies were done on the role of some well-known BMPs,  such as BMP-2, BMP-4, BMP-5, and BMP-7 in AS or TS,  but there are not any data about BMP-8a in these diseases  [25–27]. BMP-8a is induced in osteoblast differentiation and  osteogenesis phase of bone repair, and is highly expressed  in osteosarcoma [28, 29].
The plaques of TS and AS are reported to have calcium  phosphate structure [30]. Scanning electron microscopy  (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS)  can reveal the chemical structures and surface morphology  of these plaques. Koç and Üneri compared ultrastructures  of tympanosclerosis and atherosclerosis by light and elec- tron microscopy. They concluded that both specimen groups  were similar in terms of calcified area, collagen fibers, and  fibroblast [31].
As there were several similarities between the TS and AS  plaques, and also, due to controversies existed in revealing  other infective factors in pathogenesis of TS plaques [3],

Materials and methods
The proposal of the research was approved by the eth- ics committee of Guilan University of Medical Sciences  (approval code: IR.GUMS.REC, 1396.512). Eighteen TS  plaques were taken from 18 patients affected by COM  that underwent tympanoplasty/mastoidectomy surgery (11  males, 7 females, aged 42–74 years). On the other hand, 18  AS samples were taken from 18 patients suffered from AS  disease of the carotid artery that admitted for carotid endar- terectomy (14 males, 4 females, aged 48–72 years). None of  the COM cases had cholesteatoma and active otorrhea, no  one had history of previous ear surgery, and none of the TS  and AS patients received any topical or systemic antibiotics  at least 1 month before the surgery. All the patients signed  the informed consent before entering the study. After sur- gery, each sample was split into three parts for chemical,  microbial, and Immunohistochemical analyses, respectively.  To be cost-effective, only seven samples of each group were  randomly selected for SEM and EDXS analysis.
Chemical analysis
Seven samples of each group were selected for chemical  analysis. The samples were incubated in normal saline solu- tion. Topology of each plaque was assessed using SEM and  elemental analysis was done by EDXS. Chemical contents  of the plaques were compared, statistically.
Immunohistochemical analysis
Eighteen TS plaques and 18 AS plaques samples were  fixed in 10% formalin solution immediately after surgery
and paraffin blocks were prepared. Then, a 5 μm-thick sec- tions were cut and antigen retrieval was performed by heat  induced epitope retrieval (HIER). Endogenous peroxidase  activity is blocked by 1% hydrogen peroxide in methanol,  washed three times with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS),  and then incubated in blocking solution to avoid nonspecific  antibody binding. Anti-BMP8a/OP-2 antibody (Abnova,  MA, USA; dilution 1:100) was used as primary antibody  and incubated overnight at 4 °C. After three washes, the  sections incubated with polymer for 30 min. After washing,  DAB was applied as the chromogen and haematoxylin was  used as a cell nuclei counterstain. Immunostaining intensity  was evaluated by ImageJ software and compared by T test  between two groups using SPSS.
Microbial analysis and DNA extraction procedure
Once the plaque samples (18 plaques for each group) were  collected, they were placed in normal saline solution. The  plaque samples were quickly transferred to a microbiology  laboratory and immersed in liquid nitrogen. After freez- ing, they were transferred to water bath at 65 oC. Thereaf- ter, they were crushed with glass pestle. The samples were  then extracted using a DNA extraction kit (50 T-DN8115C,  SINACLON, Tehran, Iran) based on the manufacturer’s pro- tocol. The extracted DNA was used as a model for polymer- ase chain reaction (PCR). The specific primers used in the  search for these toxins and bacteria are shown in Table 1.
1 μL of the extracted DNA (400 ng/μL), and forward and  reverse primers were mixed with 10 μL (1.2 nmol) of PCR  master mix solution in a 0.2 mL microtube. The mixture was  diluted with deionized water up to 20 μL. Then, the micro- tube was placed in thermocycler. The temperature programs  are presented in Table 1s (supplemental materials). Finally,  the electrophoretic pattern of target genes was searched and  illustrated.

Results
From 18 COM cases, 9 cases had central perforations sized  30–60% of tympanic membrane (TM) surface, one case had  no obvious perforation, but showed postero-superior retrac- tion pocket with myringostapediopexy, and 8 cases had total  perforation. All the cases had dry/non-active ears for at least  3 months’ prior the surgery. The mean duration of disease  was 6 ± 2.4 years, 12 cases had bilateral COM, and the mean  of air–bone gap in tympanometry of the cases was 25 ± 7  decibel (dB). In the surgical findings, TS plaques were lim- ited to the TM in 6 cases, limited to the ossicular chain in  5 cases, and both on TM and ossicular chain in 7 cases. On  the other hand, from 18 AS cases, 12 cases had obvious  history of cardiovascular diseases for 2–12 years, 5 cases  had history of cerebrovascular diseases for 1.5–8 years, and  one case had history of recurrent claudication with 14 years’  history of hypertension.

Contrary to TS, the AS plaques show mostly needle- shaped crystalline structures (Fig. 2).
The elemental analysis of plaques (7 AS and 7 TS) by  EDXS reveals that elements forming the TS plaques were  mainly Ca, P, O, N, and C. While, AS plaques were made  of Ca, P, Cl, O, and C. Selected EDXS spectra of TS and  AS plaques are presented in Fig. 3.
The weight percent of the elements in both groups are  shown in Table 2.
According to EDXS analysis, the carbon percent of AS  plaques are significantly higher (p value: 0.004) than TS  plaques. At a significance level of 95%, calcium and phos- phorous contents of AS plaques were significantly lower  (p values < 0.05) than TS plaques. To visualize pattern  of the groups, a principal component analysis (PCA) was  applied on EDXS data. As it seems in Fig. 2s (Supplemen- tal materials), TS and AS plaques have different elemental  components.

Expression of BMP-8a of both plaques was evaluated  based on spots intensities using ImageJ software. The  expressions of BMP-8a in a plaque of AS and TS are shown  in Fig. 4.
Expression of BMP-8a in AS was ranged between 4.1 and  41.7% with the average value of 20.0 ± 9.4%. Expression  of BMP-8a in TS was from 31.6 to 73.8% with the average  value of 59.4 ± 15.2%. Comparison between expression of  BMP-8a in both diseases using t test reveals that this bone  morphogenetic protein has higher value in tympanosclerosis  (p value 5.9 × 10–9).
According to electrophoretic analysis of AS and TS  plaques (Fig. 5), ExoS gene were detected in 12 samples of  TS in comparison to 2 samples of AS. The ExoU gene test  was positive for 14 TS samples, while only 2 AS samples  had ExoU gene. The mycoplasma was positive in 3 samples  of TS and AS. The microbial toxin patterns of TS plaques  are different from those of AS plaques. Wells 43–45 show  3 positive PCR reactions for the presence of Mycoplasma  DNA in TS plaques, while wells 50, 56, and 58 indicate  3 positive PCR reactions for the presence of Mycoplasma  DNA in AS plaques (Fig. 5).
Discussion
In most occasions, calcification is present in TS plaques.  Osteoneogenesis also can happen within the middle-ear  lesions which may lead to ossicular fixation [2]. Former  studies revealed TS plaques as degenerative process, which  led to degeneration of collagen and dystrophic calcification  in connective tissue of the middle ear [1, 32]. The degenera- tion of collagen may be a direct result of inflammation or  infection within the middle ear. Although an animal study  suggested that Eustachian tube occlusion alone, without  infection, caused TS in rats [33]; other investigators showed  evidences that specific bacteria caused this disorder [3, 34,  35]. Autoimmune process had also blamed as a possible  cause of TS [36]. As mentioned, the mechanism for the for- mation of TS plaques is not clear, though many possible  mechanisms have been proposed [3, 4, 12, 36].

This could  be due to presence of myeloperoxidase (MPO) in athero- sclerotic artery. Some investigators believed that HOCl and  MPO could react with purified lipids to generate chlorinated  species.
According to the present study, the different expression  of BMP-8a in TS and AS plaques may indicate different  calcification process and pathogenesis in these two diseases.  Although BMP-8a is important in spermatogenesis, integrity  of the epididymis, and placental development [39, 40], dif- ferent studies showed that BMP-8a play a role in osteogen- esis [28, 29]. However, expression pattern of BMP family is  different in the osteogenesis [28]. Several studies showed the  involvement of different types of BMP in TS and AS plaques  [25–27]; therefore, it is plausible to play a role for BMP-8a  in the pathogenesis of these diseases.
In the present study, we showed for the first time that  BMP-8a expressed in TS and AS plaques, although this  expression was more significant in TS. It may indicate differ- ence in calcification process and pathogenesis between these  two diseases. Expressions of BMPs have been reported in  several studies related to atherosclerosis and middle-ear dis- eases. BMP-2 expression was observed significantly differ- ent in TS in contrast to chronic suppurative otitis media [27],  although BMP-2 expression is increased in the otic vesicle  of middle ears of rats with chronic suppurative otitis media  than normal rats [41]. Furthermore, it has been reported  that BMP-2 and BMP-4 play a role in vascular calcification,  promotion of endothelial dysfunction, and inflammation of  atherosclerosis [42, 43]. BMP-2, BMP-4, and BMP-6 have  been seen in vascular calcified area, whereas BMP-7 pre- vents vascular calcification [25].
There are some studies in the literature confirming the  role of bacterial infections in the pathogenesis of AS plaques  [44]. In our study, the frequency of Pseudomonas aerugi- nosa genes was higher than that of Mycoplasma genes in  patients with TS than in AS patients. This is true for both  ExoS and ExoU genes. However, the number of ExoU genes  found in TS samples was higher than the number of ExoS  samples in AS patients. The frequency of Mycoplasma genes  in both TS and AS patients was equal but less than the fre- quency of pseudomonas gene. According to the present  study, ExoU was the most abundant gene in TS patients.  This outcome has been confirmed by previous studies that  cite the frequency of genes such as ExoU is associated with  the formation of chronic otitis media infections (COM). The  genes of the bacterial type 3 secretory system (T3SS), such  as ExoS and ExoU, are associated with resistance to the anti- biotics ciprofloxacin and tobramycin [23], which are com- monly prescribed for chronic infections of the middle ear of  Pseudomonas. On the other hand, in some previous studies,
the association of the chelating role of some genes of T3SS  such as ExoS has been shown with the production of bio- films and calcium polymers [44]. This is the first time that  the probable link between the ExoU gene in calcium deposi- tion and the formation of TS plaques has been reported. The  abundance of this gene in TS patients who usually experi- ence chronic infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa could  indicate the introduction of a new link between bacteria and  calcium plaques in COM.
Conclusions
The chemical analyses of TS and AS plaques reveal that  the plaques have different elemental contents. The surface  morphologies of the plaques are also different. TS plaques  show spherical and fibril-like surfaces, while AS plaque dis- play needle-shaped surfaces. Immunohistochemical analysis  discloses that expression of BMP-8a of TS is much higher  than those of AS. Both chemical and immunohistochemical  analyses verify that different calcification process and patho- genesis are responsible for these two diseases. The microbial  analyses show that toxin producing bacteria which relate  to traffic intra/extracellular  Ca+2 might potentially relate or  alter the type or components of plaque formation. These  three methods of analysis support the idea that different  pathogenesis mechanisms and systems biology are respon- sible for occurrence of TS in comparison with AS plaques.
Study limitations
In comparative analytical study of TS and AS plaques, we  could analyze the plaques from many aspects of view, espe- cially in microbiological and immunological aspects; but  according to the previous studies in the subject, and specially  for economic limitations, we searched only for P. aeruginosa  and M. pneumoniae in both AS and TS plaques using the  PCR method. We suggest, in the future studies, other poten- tially important microorganisms and other immunologically  important mediators, furtherly being investigated.

equations.raw_extracted: Abstract Purpose The aim of this study was to compare chemical contents, expression of BMP-8a, and the presence of Mycoplasma  and ExoS-ExoU exotoxins producing Pseudomonas aeruginosa in tympanosclerosis (TS) and atherosclerosis (AS) plaques. Methods Thirty-six cases with TS and AS plaques (18 each) were selected and examined for chemical, immunohistochemi- cal, and microbial analysis. SPSS ver. 21 and t test analysis were used for comparing the findings, and the level of significance  was considered as p < 0.05. Results TS plaques showed lower carbon, higher calcium, and phosphorous contents compared to AS plaques (p value < 0.05).  Chlorine was detected in AS plaques (1.8 w%) which could probably be due to the presence of myeloperoxidase (MPO) in  atherosclerotic artery. Contrary to spherical shape of the surface of TS plaques, AS plaques were needle shaped. BMP-8a  expression in TS plaques (59.5%) was significantly higher (p value < 0.0001) than AS plaques (20%). Of the 18 TS specimens,  12, 14, and 3 were positive for ExoS, ExoU Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Mycoplasma genes, respectively, while of the 18  AS specimens, 2, 2, and 3 were positive for ExoS, ExoU Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Mycoplasma genes, respectively. Conclusion TS plaques are different from AS plaques in terms of elemental components, surface morphology, and BMP- 8a expression. Therefore, different calcification process and pathogenesis may be responsible for these two diseases. The  results of our study showed that both TS and AS plaques have genetic footprint of Mycoplasma, but the level of calcium  concentration-dependent exotoxins genes was found only in TS plaques.
Keywords Tympanosclerosis · Atherosclerosis · Scanning electron microscopy · Pseudomonas aeruginosa · BMP-8a

Tympanosclerosis (TS) is a disorder of the middle-ear cav- ity where hyaline calcareous sediments are found on the  tympanic membrane, ossicular chain, and ligaments and  occasionally in the middle ear and mastoid surfaces [1].

TS plaques within the tympanic membrane often appear  as a semicircular crescent white plaque within the tym- panic membrane [2]. The prevalence of tympanosclerosis  in chronic otitis media (COM) has been reported from 9 to  38%. Relative to the quantity of calcification and its distur- bance of the ossicular chain movement, the patients experi- ence different degrees of conductive hearing loss. The etiol- ogy of TS has not been revealed completely [3]. However,  infection, physical trauma, myringotomy incisions, applica- tion of ventilation tube, chemical agents, metabolic changes,  genetic factors, and immunological reactions are considered  as responsible factors for this disease [4].

Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease  characterized by accumulation of lipids together with pen- etration of immunocytes, inflammatory cells, and calcium  deposits in the walls of medium and large-sized arteries,  wherein the arterial walls become thicker and lose their elas- ticity [5]. Endothelial cells, intimate smooth muscle cells,  and leukocytes have key roles in the progress of AS [6].  AS is a slow advancing and progressive disease, starting  from childhood. Various factors have been suggested as the  cause of this disease including hyperlipidemia, hypertension,  smoking, infection with bacteria and viruses, diabetes mel- litus, obesity, and genetic and habitual factors [7, 8].

Although TS and AS appears in two different organs,  they share similar histopathological and physiopathological  elements, and historically, many experts have known these  two processes as identical [9]. In both diseases, it is not  precisely recognized what starts the lesion principally [10].  Interestingly, some previous studies revealed relationship  between these diseases, and showed that AS patients had sta- tistically significant rate of TS in comparison to the normal  population. Pirodda et al. showed around 22.5% of hyper- cholesterolemia patients (4.9% in control subjects) and 36%  of patients underwent carotid endarterectomy (12% in con- trol group) had TS on otoscopy [10, 11]. In another study,  homocysteine, low-density lipoprotein, total cholesterol, and  triglyceride levels in 61 COM patients with TS plaques were  higher compared with those without TS plaques (p < 0.05)  and right and left internal carotid artery intima-media thick- ness was greater significantly (p = 0.001). In conclusion,  AS and TS were associated with identical risk factors [12].  These studies emphasized that there must be similar risk  factors triggering pathogenesis in both diseases [13].

TS is a progressive disorder, which appears to be the  main response of the tympanic membrane pars tensa to pro- longed sterile otitis media with effusion [14], and most of  the patients suffering from TS have earlier exposure to recur- rent serous otitis media (SOM), acute otitis media (AOM),  or chronic otitis media (COM) [15]. According to previous  studies, nitric oxide, free oxygen radicals, and catalase may  have a role in the development of TS in COM [16, 17]. Some  other studies revealed that the alteration in expressions of

transforming growth factor β1 (TGF-β1) and matrix metal- loproteinase-9 (MMP-9) involved in the formation of TS,  which may represent an important mechanism underlying  the pathogenesis of TS [18, 19]. Another study declared that  an association between C. pneumoniae or H. pylori infection  and the development of TS or other types of COM could not  be established [3]. Also, it has been generally believed that  bacteria such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Mycoplasma  pneumoniae involve in AOM and COM as well as in occur- rence of inflammatory process such as AS. Mycoplasma  pneumonia causes common respiratory tract infections, and  up to one-third of patients with Mycoplasma pneumonia  infection may have ear infection, although without positive  middle-ear fluid PCR [19]. This may partly be caused by dif- ficulties in culturing this fastidious organism. Nevertheless,  otitis media is often mentioned as a clinical condition asso- ciated with serologically verified M. pneumoniae infection.  Many studies in the past have shown the presence of Myco- plasma in cardiovascular diseases and middle-ear infections  in children and adults [20, 21].
The toxins such as ExoS and ExoU which are secreted  by type 3 secretion system (T3SS) of bacteria are the key  component responsible for TS, AOM, and COM [22, 23].

Due to development of calcification in both diseases,  evaluation of bone remodeling markers is a priority for  understanding the pathogenesis of these diseases. Different  factors influence differentiation and activation of osteoblasts,  and one of the most important ones is bone morphogenetic  proteins (BMPs). BMPs are the largest family of the TGF-β  superfamily and originally were recognized for their abil- ity in induction of bone formation, but it has known they  expressed in many tissues and have a role in a wide range  of processes including cellular proliferation and differen- tiation, adipogenesis, skeletal development, formation and  maintenance of vascular systems, and cancers [24]. A few  studies were done on the role of some well-known BMPs,  such as BMP-2, BMP-4, BMP-5, and BMP-7 in AS or TS,  but there are not any data about BMP-8a in these diseases  [25–27]. BMP-8a is induced in osteoblast differentiation and  osteogenesis phase of bone repair, and is highly expressed  in osteosarcoma [28, 29].

The plaques of TS and AS are reported to have calcium  phosphate structure [30]. Scanning electron microscopy  (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS)  can reveal the chemical structures and surface morphology  of these plaques. Koç and Üneri compared ultrastructures  of tympanosclerosis and atherosclerosis by light and elec- tron microscopy. They concluded that both specimen groups  were similar in terms of calcified area, collagen fibers, and  fibroblast [31].
As there were several similarities between the TS and AS  plaques, and also, due to controversies existed in revealing  other infective factors in pathogenesis of TS plaques [3],

the present study attempted to explore chemical identities  and morphologies, assay BMP-8a level, as well as analyze  some new microbial contents of the AS and TS plaques. We  thought the study of the relationship between bacteria pre- sent both in middle-ear infection and cardiovascular diseases  and their virulence factors could provide new evidence of  the etiological relationship of these diseases.

The proposal of the research was approved by the eth- ics committee of Guilan University of Medical Sciences  (approval code: IR.GUMS.REC, 1396.512). Eighteen TS  plaques were taken from 18 patients affected by COM  that underwent tympanoplasty/mastoidectomy surgery (11  males, 7 females, aged 42–74 years). On the other hand, 18  AS samples were taken from 18 patients suffered from AS  disease of the carotid artery that admitted for carotid endar- terectomy (14 males, 4 females, aged 48–72 years). None of  the COM cases had cholesteatoma and active otorrhea, no  one had history of previous ear surgery, and none of the TS  and AS patients received any topical or systemic antibiotics  at least 1 month before the surgery. All the patients signed  the informed consent before entering the study. After sur- gery, each sample was split into three parts for chemical,  microbial, and Immunohistochemical analyses, respectively.  To be cost-effective, only seven samples of each group were  randomly selected for SEM and EDXS analysis.

Seven samples of each group were selected for chemical  analysis. The samples were incubated in normal saline solu- tion. Topology of each plaque was assessed using SEM and  elemental analysis was done by EDXS. Chemical contents  of the plaques were compared, statistically.
Eighteen TS plaques and 18 AS plaques samples were  fixed in 10% formalin solution immediately after surgery

and paraffin blocks were prepared. Then, a 5 μm-thick sec- tions were cut and antigen retrieval was performed by heat  induced epitope retrieval (HIER). Endogenous peroxidase  activity is blocked by 1% hydrogen peroxide in methanol,  washed three times with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS),  and then incubated in blocking solution to avoid nonspecific  antibody binding. Anti-BMP8a/OP-2 antibody (Abnova,  MA, USA; dilution 1:100) was used as primary antibody  and incubated overnight at 4 °C. After three washes, the  sections incubated with polymer for 30 min. After washing,  DAB was applied as the chromogen and haematoxylin was  used as a cell nuclei counterstain. Immunostaining intensity  was evaluated by ImageJ software and compared by T test  between two groups using SPSS.

Once the plaque samples (18 plaques for each group) were  collected, they were placed in normal saline solution. The  plaque samples were quickly transferred to a microbiology  laboratory and immersed in liquid nitrogen. After freez- ing, they were transferred to water bath at 65 oC. Thereaf- ter, they were crushed with glass pestle. The samples were  then extracted using a DNA extraction kit (50 T-DN8115C,  SINACLON, Tehran, Iran) based on the manufacturer’s pro- tocol. The extracted DNA was used as a model for polymer- ase chain reaction (PCR). The specific primers used in the  search for these toxins and bacteria are shown in Table 1.

1 μL of the extracted DNA (400 ng/μL), and forward and  reverse primers were mixed with 10 μL (1.2 nmol) of PCR  master mix solution in a 0.2 mL microtube. The mixture was  diluted with deionized water up to 20 μL. Then, the micro- tube was placed in thermocycler. The temperature programs  are presented in Table 1s (supplemental materials). Finally,  the electrophoretic pattern of target genes was searched and  illustrated.

From 18 COM cases, 9 cases had central perforations sized  30–60% of tympanic membrane (TM) surface, one case had  no obvious perforation, but showed postero-superior retrac- tion pocket with myringostapediopexy, and 8 cases had total  perforation. Contrary to TS, the AS plaques show mostly needle- shaped crystalline structures (Fig. 2).

The elemental analysis of plaques (7 AS and 7 TS) by  EDXS reveals that elements forming the TS plaques were  mainly Ca, P, O, N, and C. While, AS plaques were made  of Ca, P, Cl, O, and C. Selected EDXS spectra of TS and  AS plaques are presented in Fig. 3.
The weight percent of the elements in both groups are  shown in Table 2.

According to EDXS analysis, the carbon percent of AS  plaques are significantly higher (p value: 0.004) than TS  plaques. At a significance level of 95%, calcium and phos- phorous contents of AS plaques were significantly lower  (p values < 0.05) than TS plaques. To visualize pattern  of the groups, a principal component analysis (PCA) was  applied on EDXS data. As it seems in Fig. 2s (Supplemen- tal materials), TS and AS plaques have different elemental  components.

Expression of BMP-8a of both plaques was evaluated  based on spots intensities using ImageJ software. The  expressions of BMP-8a in a plaque of AS and TS are shown  in Fig. 4.

Expression of BMP-8a in AS was ranged between 4.1 and  41.7% with the average value of 20.0 ± 9.4%. Expression  of BMP-8a in TS was from 31.6 to 73.8% with the average  value of 59.4 ± 15.2%. Comparison between expression of  BMP-8a in both diseases using t test reveals that this bone  morphogenetic protein has higher value in tympanosclerosis  (p value 5.9 × 10–9).

According to electrophoretic analysis of AS and TS  plaques (Fig. 5), ExoS gene were detected in 12 samples of  TS in comparison to 2 samples of AS. The ExoU gene test  was positive for 14 TS samples, while only 2 AS samples  had ExoU gene. The mycoplasma was positive in 3 samples  of TS and AS. The microbial toxin patterns of TS plaques  are different from those of AS plaques. Wells 43–45 show  3 positive PCR reactions for the presence of Mycoplasma  DNA in TS plaques, while wells 50, 56, and 58 indicate  3 positive PCR reactions for the presence of Mycoplasma  DNA in AS plaques (Fig. 5).

In most occasions, calcification is present in TS plaques.  Osteoneogenesis also can happen within the middle-ear  lesions which may lead to ossicular fixation [2]. Former  studies revealed TS plaques as degenerative process, which  led to degeneration of collagen and dystrophic calcification  in connective tissue of the middle ear [1, 32]. The degenera- tion of collagen may be a direct result of inflammation or  infection within the middle ear. Although an animal study  suggested that Eustachian tube occlusion alone, without  infection, caused TS in rats [33]; other investigators showed  evidences that specific bacteria caused this disorder [3, 34,  35]. Autoimmune process had also blamed as a possible  cause of TS [36]. As mentioned, the mechanism for the for- mation of TS plaques is not clear, though many possible  mechanisms have been proposed [3, 4, 12, 36].

According to the present study, the different expression  of BMP-8a in TS and AS plaques may indicate different  calcification process and pathogenesis in these two diseases.  Although BMP-8a is important in spermatogenesis, integrity  of the epididymis, and placental development [39, 40], dif- ferent studies showed that BMP-8a play a role in osteogen- esis [28, 29]. However, expression pattern of BMP family is  different in the osteogenesis [28]. Several studies showed the  involvement of different types of BMP in TS and AS plaques  [25–27]; therefore, it is plausible to play a role for BMP-8a  in the pathogenesis of these diseases.

In the present study, we showed for the first time that  BMP-8a expressed in TS and AS plaques, although this  expression was more significant in TS. It may indicate differ- ence in calcification process and pathogenesis between these  two diseases. Expressions of BMPs have been reported in  several studies related to atherosclerosis and middle-ear dis- eases. BMP-2 expression was observed significantly differ- ent in TS in contrast to chronic suppurative otitis media [27],  although BMP-2 expression is increased in the otic vesicle  of middle ears of rats with chronic suppurative otitis media  than normal rats [41]. Furthermore, it has been reported  that BMP-2 and BMP-4 play a role in vascular calcification,  promotion of endothelial dysfunction, and inflammation of  atherosclerosis [42, 43]. BMP-2, BMP-4, and BMP-6 have  been seen in vascular calcified area, whereas BMP-7 pre- vents vascular calcification [25].

There are some studies in the literature confirming the  role of bacterial infections in the pathogenesis of AS plaques  [44]. In our study, the frequency of Pseudomonas aerugi- nosa genes was higher than that of Mycoplasma genes in  patients with TS than in AS patients. This is true for both  ExoS and ExoU genes. However, the number of ExoU genes  found in TS samples was higher than the number of ExoS  samples in AS patients. The frequency of Mycoplasma genes  in both TS and AS patients was equal but less than the fre- quency of pseudomonas gene. According to the present  study, ExoU was the most abundant gene in TS patients.  This outcome has been confirmed by previous studies that  cite the frequency of genes such as ExoU is associated with  the formation of chronic otitis media infections (COM). The  genes of the bacterial type 3 secretory system (T3SS), such  as ExoS and ExoU, are associated with resistance to the anti- biotics ciprofloxacin and tobramycin [23], which are com- monly prescribed for chronic infections of the middle ear of  Pseudomonas. On the other hand, in some previous studies,

the association of the chelating role of some genes of T3SS  such as ExoS has been shown with the production of bio- films and calcium polymers [44]. This is the first time that  the probable link between the ExoU gene in calcium deposi- tion and the formation of TS plaques has been reported. The  abundance of this gene in TS patients who usually experi- ence chronic infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa could  indicate the introduction of a new link between bacteria and  calcium plaques in COM.

The chemical analyses of TS and AS plaques reveal that  the plaques have different elemental contents. The surface  morphologies of the plaques are also different. TS plaques  show spherical and fibril-like surfaces, while AS plaque dis- play needle-shaped surfaces. Immunohistochemical analysis  discloses that expression of BMP-8a of TS is much higher  than those of AS. Both chemical and immunohistochemical  analyses verify that different calcification process and patho- genesis are responsible for these two diseases. The microbial  analyses show that toxin producing bacteria which relate  to traffic intra/extracellular  Ca+2 might potentially relate or  alter the type or components of plaque formation. These  three methods of analysis support the idea that different  pathogenesis mechanisms and systems biology are respon- sible for occurrence of TS in comparison with AS plaques.

In comparative analytical study of TS and AS plaques, we  could analyze the plaques from many aspects of view, espe- cially in microbiological and immunological aspects; but  according to the previous studies in the subject, and specially  for economic limitations, we searched only for P. aeruginosa  and M. pneumoniae in both AS and TS plaques using the  PCR method. We suggest, in the future studies, other poten- tially important microorganisms and other immunologically  important mediators, furtherly being investigated.
